nameStory: This tiny water flea gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'broad-tailed' (Eurycercus) and 'long-snouted' (longirostris). If you could see one under a microscope, you'd notice its distinctively wide, flattened tail area and elongated 'nose' that help it navigate through pond water like a microscopic submarine.
description: The long-snouted water flea is a microscopic freshwater crustacean that's barely visible to the naked eye, measuring only about 1-3 millimeters long. Despite being called a 'flea,' it's actually more closely related to shrimp and crabs than to insects. This translucent creature has a distinctive teardrop shape with large compound eyes and uses its branched antennae like oars to swim through pond water. You'll need a magnifying glass or microscope to really appreciate its intricate details.

idTips.label: Elongated rostrum
idTips.description: Under magnification, look for the pointed 'beak' or snout extending from the front of the head - much longer and more pronounced than other water fleas

idTips.label: Broad tail region
idTips.description: The rear portion appears noticeably wide and flattened compared to the narrow front end, giving it an asymmetrical teardrop shape

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves through water with distinctive jerky, hopping motions rather than smooth gliding, using large antennae as paddles

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Typically 2-3 millimeters long - larger than many other water fleas but still requiring magnification to see clearly

idTips.label: Transparent body
idTips.description: Body appears glass-like and colorless, though you may see dark spots of the digestive system through the clear shell

habitat: Look for these microscopic creatures in shallow, weedy areas of ponds, slow-moving streams, and lake margins throughout New England. They prefer areas with aquatic vegetation where they can graze on algae and organic debris. You're most likely to find them in the top few feet of water where sunlight supports plant growth.

seasonality.spring: Population begins building as water warms above 50°F. Best time to find them as they become active after winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance in warm water. Look for them during early morning or evening when they may venture closer to the surface.
seasonality.fall: Still active but populations declining. They begin producing dormant eggs that will survive winter freezing.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off in freezing conditions, surviving only as dormant eggs in pond sediments until spring thaw.

funFact: Despite having one of the most sophisticated visual systems among microscopic creatures - with compound eyes containing dozens of lenses - these water fleas are essentially living in a world of giants, where a minnow appears as massive as a blue whale would to us.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other water fleas like Daphnia, but remember the 'Pinocchio nose' - that long snout is your dead giveaway that you've found a Eurycercus rather than its round-headed cousins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'water fleas,' these creatures are actually tiny crustaceans more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to any kind of flea or insect. The name comes from their jerky swimming motion that resembles a flea's hopping movement.
compareHints: This is the only Eurycercus species commonly found in New England waters. Compared to other water fleas in the region, it's distinguished by its much longer rostrum and broader tail section. While Daphnia species have rounded heads and compact bodies, Eurycercus longirostris has that unmistakable elongated snout that extends well beyond its antennae bases.
